1.title: Development includes gains and constraints.
points: Development: change and continuity across life
Plasticity: capacity for change under conditions
Context: social and historical circumstances
1.text:
Development: change and continuity across life. Plasticity: capacity for change under conditions. Context: social and historical circumstances.

Developmental psychology studies patterns of change and continuity from before birth through later life. Gains in one skill can accompany costs in another.

Jo and Pat differ in experience as well as age. The café episode does not identify an age effect or either person’s general ability.

sections.heading: The research question
sections.text: Distinguish an age difference from evidence of developmental change and propose a better comparison.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Lifespan research treats development as multidirectional and embedded in historical contexts. Average age trends summarize samples; they do not fix an individual’s trajectory.

Selective samples, repeated testing and changing environments limit causal claims. The fictional café comparison illustrates those limits; it is not developmental data.

sections.heading: The example and its limits
sections.text: The café and transfer cases are original fictional examples, not participants or results from the cited studies. The case varies age and experience together; it cannot isolate development.

1.title: Age groups are not a time machine.
points: Cross-sectional study: compares age groups at one time
Cohort: people sharing a historical period
Longitudinal study: follows the same people over time
1.text:
Cross-sectional study: compares age groups at one time. Cohort: people sharing a historical period.

A cross-sectional comparison can reveal age differences, but cohorts may differ in schooling or technology exposure. A longitudinal study can examine within-person change.

Longitudinal findings can still reflect repeated testing and selective dropout. Combining designs helps distinguish age, history and measurement effects.

1.title: Describe the task before the person.
points: Measurement: a defined way of recording an outcome
Practice effect: change from taking a task again
Attrition: loss of participants over time
1.text:
Measurement: a defined way of recording an outcome. Practice effect: change from taking a task again. Attrition: loss of participants over time.

Record learning accuracy, time and prior experience on comparable tasks. Follow change rather than ranking the worth of age groups.

An accessible display may help Pat immediately without changing an underlying ability. Developmental explanations need evidence about the task, the environment and the person over time.

2.title: Development starts before birth.
points: Prenatal development: development before birth
Gestation: the course of pregnancy
Teratogen: an exposure that can disrupt prenatal development
2.text:
Gestation: the course of pregnancy. Teratogen: an exposure that can disrupt prenatal development.

Prenatal development involves changing biological systems. Some exposures can increase the risk of harm, and effects depend partly on when development is occurring.

This does not mean an exposure guarantees an outcome. Advice about a specific pregnancy belongs with a qualified healthcare professional who can evaluate the actual exposure.

sections.heading: The research question
sections.text: Explain how timing, dose and context qualify a prenatal risk claim.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Prenatal risk evidence often comes from observational studies because harmful exposures cannot ethically be assigned. Confounding, exposure measurement and differences between outcomes matter.

A sensitive period is specific to a system and experience. It does not mean that all development ends after an early deadline.

sections.heading: The example and its limits
sections.text: The café and transfer cases are original fictional examples, not participants or results from the cited studies. A general risk claim cannot determine an individual pregnancy outcome.

2.title: Timing changes the question.
points: Sensitive period: time of heightened responsiveness
Dose: amount of exposure
Risk factor: condition associated with increased likelihood
2.text:
Sensitive period: time of heightened responsiveness. Risk factor: condition associated with increased likelihood.

A developing system can be more responsive to an exposure during particular periods. Dose, duration, nutrition, health and other exposures may also matter.

A population association does not show which factor caused a particular child’s difficulty. Retrospective accounts can leave important details unmeasured.

2.title: Support changes a developmental pathway.
points: Protective factor: condition that can reduce adverse risk
Probabilistic: concerning likelihood rather than certainty
Developmental pathway: pattern of change over time
2.text:
Protective factor: condition that can reduce adverse risk. Probabilistic: concerning likelihood rather than certainty. Developmental pathway: pattern of change over time.

Healthcare access and supportive environments can influence later opportunities. Biological and social development continue to interact after birth.

Avoid assigning blame from a simplified origin story. Ask what is known now and which practical supports are appropriate, without promising that support reverses every possible effect.

3.title: Infants provide indirect evidence.
points: Habituation: reduced responding with repeated stimulation
Dishabituation: renewed responding after a change
Looking time: duration of visual attention
3.text:
Habituation: reduced responding with repeated stimulation. Dishabituation: renewed responding after a change. Looking time: duration of visual attention.

Infants cannot explain an answer verbally. Researchers therefore use responses such as looking, reaching or sucking under defined conditions.

A renewed look can indicate discrimination or novelty. It does not by itself reveal a complete adult-like concept. Visual salience and familiarity are alternative explanations to test.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Infant methods provide valuable evidence when comparison events control low-level differences and results replicate. Different measures can produce different developmental estimates.

The fictional toy event does not demonstrate a universal timetable, intelligence score or diagnosis.

3.title: Different tasks ask different questions.
points: Object permanence: understanding that objects continue unseen
Task demand: what successful performance requires
Converging evidence: support from different suitable methods
3.text:
Object permanence: understanding that objects continue unseen. Task demand: what successful performance requires.

Searching for a hidden object requires remembering a location and coordinating action. A looking task has different demands.

Different ages of success across tasks need not mean one method is useless. Compare the specific ability each task requires and seek converging evidence before making a broad claim.

3.title: Early learning is active and situated.
points: Joint attention: sharing attention toward something
Contingent response: response related to a preceding signal
Individual variation: differences among developmental paths
3.text:
Joint attention: sharing attention toward something. Contingent response: response related to a preceding signal. Individual variation: differences among developmental paths.

Infants learn through perception, movement and interaction with caregivers. Shared attention can support learning about objects and words.

Developmental milestones describe useful patterns of change, with variation. A casual observation is not a developmental assessment. Persistent concerns are a reason to seek appropriate professional advice.

4.title: Thinking changes through activity.
points: Schema: organized understanding of a situation
Assimilation: interpreting experience using an existing schema
Accommodation: changing a schema to fit experience
4.text:
Schema: organized understanding of a situation. Assimilation: interpreting experience using an existing schema. Accommodation: changing a schema to fit experience.

Piaget described children as actively constructing understanding. New experiences can fit an existing way of thinking or require revising it.

His broad stages remain historically influential, but performance also varies with task wording, experience and support. Do not use a stage label as a complete account of a particular child.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Developmental theories guide questions rather than establish rigid instructions for every age. Evidence on guided learning depends on how assistance and later transfer are measured.

The café task is an illustration. It does not validate a teaching method for all learners or make a developmental assessment.

4.title: Help can reveal a learning opportunity.
points: Zone of proximal development: gap between independent and supported performance
Scaffolding: temporary support adjusted to a task
Guided participation: learning through supported shared activity
4.text:
Zone of proximal development: gap between independent and supported performance. Scaffolding: temporary support adjusted to a task. Guided participation: learning through supported shared activity.

Vygotsky emphasized learning in social and cultural activity. Success with guidance identifies what is possible with that support.

Jo can model one comparison, invite the visitor to explain, then reduce help. Independent performance needs a later attempt without the prompt and a suitable new example.

4.title: Language grows in interaction.
points: Receptive language: understanding communicated language
Expressive language: producing communicated language
Bilingual development: development involving more than one language
4.text:
Receptive language: understanding communicated language. Expressive language: producing communicated language. Bilingual development: development involving more than one language.

Understanding and producing words are different demands. Vocabulary in each language depends on exposure and context; a single-language count can miss knowledge expressed elsewhere.

Invite clear, responsive communication rather than judging ability from one conversation. Concerns about development require culturally and linguistically appropriate assessment.

5.title: Closeness can support exploration.
points: Attachment: a bond supporting proximity and safety
Secure base: a caregiver relationship supporting exploration
Safe haven: comfort sought when distressed
5.text:
Secure base: a caregiver relationship supporting exploration. Safe haven: comfort sought when distressed.

Attachment theory concerns how relationships support safety and exploration, particularly under stress. Staying close in an unfamiliar room can have several explanations.

A short café visit cannot classify a child or caregiver. Researchers use structured procedures and consider the relationship and context being measured.

sections.heading: The research question
sections.text: Explain attachment as a context-sensitive relationship pattern without assigning a fixed identity.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Attachment evidence uses relationship-specific measures and longitudinal comparisons. Cultural practices, measurement and stress conditions affect interpretation.

Early associations with later outcomes are probabilistic. They do not show that one behavior identifies a permanent attachment style or parental fault.

sections.heading: The example and its limits
sections.text: The café and transfer cases are original fictional examples, not participants or results from the cited studies. The sequence is illustrative, not an assessment of attachment security.

5.title: A pattern is not an identity.
points: Attachment pattern: observed relationship-related organization
Temperament: early differences in reactivity and regulation
Caregiving sensitivity: noticing and responding appropriately to signals
5.text:
Attachment pattern: observed relationship-related organization. Caregiving sensitivity: noticing and responding appropriately to signals.

Temperament and attachment address different questions. A child may react strongly to noise without having an insecure relationship.

Attachment classifications summarize behavior in specified circumstances. They are not moral ratings, permanent personality types or diagnoses from a single behavior.

5.title: Relationships develop in wider conditions.
points: Responsiveness: appropriate response to another’s signals
Continuity: persistence across time
Change: variation in later relationship experience
5.text:
Responsiveness: appropriate response to another’s signals. Continuity: persistence across time. Change: variation in later relationship experience.

Responsive care matters, but caregiving occurs within work, health, housing and cultural conditions. Children can form attachments with more than one caregiver.

Early patterns can be associated with later outcomes without determining them. Later relationships and changing circumstances also contribute to development.

6.title: Development has connected settings.
points: Microsystem: immediate setting and relationships
Mesosystem: connections between immediate settings
Ecological approach: development within interacting contexts
6.text:
Microsystem: immediate setting and relationships. Mesosystem: connections between immediate settings.

An ecological approach examines the child in family, school, peer and community settings. Links between those settings can influence experience.

A quiet response at the café may reflect unfamiliar language, relationships or task expectations. A parenting explanation is one possible account, not a finding established by the observation.

sections.heading: The research question
sections.text: Identify interacting contexts that could contribute to a developmental observation.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Ecological models organize possible influences; drawing a map does not prove every proposed causal arrow. Observational associations need careful interpretation.

Culture, resources and structural constraints qualify comparisons of family practices. One preferred family style is not a universal explanation of outcomes.

sections.heading: The example and its limits
sections.text: The café and transfer cases are original fictional examples, not participants or results from the cited studies. Different contexts supply different opportunities to participate.

6.title: Influences can run both ways.
points: Bidirectional influence: each participant affects the other
Selection effect: people enter different environments
Confounding: another factor contributes to an association
6.text:
Bidirectional influence: each participant affects the other. Selection effect: people enter different environments. Confounding: another factor contributes to an association.

Children affect adult responses while adults shape children’s opportunities. Family stress, resources and individual characteristics may influence both.

A correlation between a parenting measure and behavior does not isolate a one-way cause. Stronger designs examine alternative explanations and change over time.

6.title: Peers can support different behaviors.
points: Peer norm: expectation within a peer group
Socialization: learning shared practices and expectations
Exosystem: settings affecting a child indirectly
6.text:
Peer norm: expectation within a peer group. Socialization: learning shared practices and expectations. Exosystem: settings affecting a child indirectly.

Peers can encourage participation, practice and belonging, as well as pressure toward risky actions. The effect depends on the group and situation.

An adult’s work schedule may change a child’s available support indirectly. Examine specific conditions before turning a contextual pattern into a judgment about a family.

7.title: Development is uneven and contextual.
points: Puberty: biological changes toward sexual maturation
Adolescence: transition involving biological and social changes
Self-regulation: regulating attention, emotion and action
7.text:
Self-regulation: regulating attention, emotion and action.

Puberty and adolescence are related but not identical. Physical development, opportunities and social expectations can change on different schedules.

Adolescents often show sophisticated reasoning. Decision quality varies with experience, arousal, incentives and social context. Average developmental patterns do not determine an individual’s competence.

7.title: Peers and opportunities shape decisions.
points: Peer influence: effects of peers on judgments or actions
Identity exploration: considering roles, values and commitments
Autonomy: acting with meaningful self-direction
7.text:
Peer influence: effects of peers on judgments or actions.

Peers can encourage care and competence as well as risk. Identity exploration and growing autonomy can support learning and responsibility.

Offer real choices within clear safety boundaries. A supervised practice opportunity can teach a skill more directly than an age stereotype or a vague demand to be sensible.

7.title: Brain images do not set a universal birthday.
points: Group average: summary across a sample
Individual variability: differences within an age group
Developmental trajectory: pattern of change over time
7.text:
Group average: summary across a sample. Individual variability: differences within an age group. Developmental trajectory: pattern of change over time.

Brain development continues across adolescence and adulthood, but different measures follow different trajectories. There is no single measurement that marks every person as fully developed at a particular birthday.

A group brain finding does not determine legal or practical competence by itself. Specify the actual decision and its demands.

8.title: A life path is not one universal sequence.
points: Social clock: cultural expectations about timing
Life transition: change in roles or circumstances
Life course: a trajectory embedded in history and society
8.text:
Social clock: cultural expectations about timing. Life transition: change in roles or circumstances. Life course: a trajectory embedded in history and society.

Education, work, partnership and caring roles occur in different orders and at different times. Norms about timing depend on social conditions and culture.

A transition can offer opportunities and strain. Being unusual relative to a local expectation is not evidence of developmental failure.

sections.heading: What the sources support
sections.text:
Lifespan models describe varied pathways rather than prescribe a single life timetable. Much adult-development evidence is observational and shaped by historical opportunity.

An adaptation framework does not establish that every constraint can be overcome through effort or attitude.

8.title: Roles interact with resources.
points: Role strain: difficulty meeting demands of a role
Linked lives: interdependence of life trajectories
Selection: choosing goals or activities
8.text:
Role strain: difficulty meeting demands of a role. Linked lives: interdependence of life trajectories. Selection: choosing goals or activities.

A return to study depends on money, care responsibilities, health and opportunity as well as motivation. Changes in one person’s work can affect the whole household.

Ask which demands changed and which resources are available. An individual preference does not explain every constraint or outcome.

8.title: Adaptation can change the goal or the route.
points: Optimization: investing resources in a selected goal
Compensation: using another method when a route is limited
Agency: capacity to act within circumstances
8.text:
Optimization: investing resources in a selected goal. Compensation: using another method when a route is limited. Agency: capacity to act within circumstances.

Lifespan accounts distinguish selecting goals, optimizing resources and compensating for constraints. Pat may choose fewer projects, practise a new skill and use an accessible tool.

These are descriptive strategies, not a promise that individuals can overcome every structural barrier. Support and access remain part of the explanation.

9.title: Abilities do not change as one block.
points: Fluid abilities: reasoning with relatively novel information
Crystallized abilities: accumulated knowledge and skills
Processing speed: speed of specified cognitive operations
9.text:
Fluid abilities: reasoning with relatively novel information. Crystallized abilities: accumulated knowledge and skills. Processing speed: speed of specified cognitive operations.

Some average cognitive measures change earlier or more strongly than others. Accumulated knowledge can remain useful while speed on unfamiliar tasks changes.

Education, health, sensory access and experience influence performance. A broad age trend cannot diagnose Pat or predict every skill.

A course cannot evaluate a person’s cognition. The fictional menu task provides no diagnostic evidence.

9.title: Access can change performance.
points: Sensory access: ability to receive task information
Compensatory aid: tool supporting a limited route
Within-person change: difference from an individual’s earlier performance
9.text:
Sensory access: ability to receive task information. Compensatory aid: tool supporting a limited route. Within-person change: difference from an individual’s earlier performance.

Small print, hearing difficulty and unfamiliar controls can raise task demands. An accessible display and written sequence may improve performance immediately.

Persistent or concerning changes in memory or daily functioning deserve qualified assessment. Ordinary mistakes alone do not establish a neurocognitive disorder.

9.title: Wellbeing has social conditions.
points: Ageism: stereotyping or discrimination based on age
Social participation: involvement in relationships and activities
Heterogeneity: substantial variation within a group
9.text:
Ageism: stereotyping or discrimination based on age. Social participation: involvement in relationships and activities. Heterogeneity: substantial variation within a group.

Later life includes wide variation in health, resources, relationships and preferences. Exclusion can remove opportunities to practise and contribute.

Invite Pat to choose useful support rather than assuming either inability or unlimited resilience. A respectful response combines agency with attention to actual needs.

10.title: Connect time with context.
points: Continuity: persistence in a developmental pattern
Discontinuity: a qualitative change in a pattern
Transactional account: person and environment influence each other over time
10.text:
Continuity: persistence in a developmental pattern. Discontinuity: a qualitative change in a pattern. Transactional account: person and environment influence each other over time.

A developmental explanation asks what changed, for whom, in which setting and over what period. Stable patterns can coexist with change in particular skills.

The same workshop outcome can reflect prior experience, access, relationships and instruction. Explain the proposed mechanism instead of substituting an age label.

Course completion and self-confidence are not evidence of professional competence. An unfamiliar later case provides a more useful learning check.

10.title: Evaluate support against an outcome.
points: Intervention: planned change intended to affect an outcome
Transfer: use in a different situation
Follow-up: measurement after time has passed
10.text:
Intervention: planned change intended to affect an outcome. Transfer: use in a different situation. Follow-up: measurement after time has passed.

Choose a support that addresses a specific demand, such as a clear example or accessible instructions. Define the intended outcome before judging success.

Compare comparable conditions, check an unfamiliar example and revisit later. Immediate participation is useful evidence, but it does not establish durable independent learning.

10.title: Use knowledge without claiming authority over people.
points: Consent: freely given agreement to participation
Privacy: control over personal information
Proportionate inference: conclusion limited to the evidence
10.text:
Consent: freely given agreement to participation. Privacy: control over personal information. Proportionate inference: conclusion limited to the evidence.

Developmental ideas can make instructions more accessible and interpretations more careful. They do not authorize informal diagnosis, surveillance or experiments on children.

Use fictional cases or your own low-stakes tasks for practice. For genuine developmental or health concerns, seek relevant professional advice rather than assigning a label.
